title: Impact desk
kicker: 1.6 Ethical, legal, cultural and environmental impacts  |  Lesson 1
subtitle: OCR J277 Paper 1  |  Computer systems
intro: The six kinds of impact every new technology has, and how to argue an ethical question properly.
objectives: know the range of issues to consider when a new technology is introduced
understand at least one ethical issue of computer technology
be able to argue both sides and reach a conclusion
starter: Think of a technology released in your lifetime that made something worse as well as better. What was gained, and what was lost?
keyq: What should be considered before a new technology is introduced?

stations.name: Beyond building it
bullets: A new system is judged on far more than whether it works.
Six kinds of impact come up again and again: ethical, legal, cultural, environmental, privacy and the wider effect on society.
Most real decisions involve several at once, pulling in different directions.
stations.challenge: Name the six kinds of impact, and give an example of each in one line.

stations.name: Ethical issues
bullets: An ethical issue asks whether something should be done, not whether it can be.
Examples: tracking people's location, using AI to mark exams, selling data about children, automating jobs away.
There is rarely one right answer, which is why the exam asks you to discuss both sides.
stations.challenge: Write one ethical question raised by a technology you use, and one argument each way.

stations.name: Two sides of an argument
bullets: A good answer gives arguments for, arguments against, and a conclusion you can defend.
Each argument needs a reason and, ideally, who it affects.
'It's bad' is not an argument. 'It's bad because…, which harms…' is.
stations.challenge: Write one argument for and one against schools monitoring what pupils type.

stations.name: Stakeholders
bullets: A stakeholder is anyone affected by a system: users, staff, customers, the wider public.
The same change helps some stakeholders and harms others.
Naming the stakeholders is usually the first mark in an impact question.
stations.challenge: List four stakeholders affected by a school introducing cashless payments.

stations.name: Piracy: a worked example
bullets: Copying films, music, games or software without paying is illegal, and it is also an ethical question.
For: content is expensive, some is unavailable legally, one copy costs the maker nothing extra.
Against: creators lose income, studios make fewer risky projects, the money funds crime.
stations.challenge: Write your own conclusion on piracy, and justify it in two sentences.

stations.name: Writing the answer
bullets: Name the impact: ethical, legal, cultural, environmental, privacy.
Name the stakeholders and say how each is affected.
Give both sides, then conclude.
stations.challenge: Plan an eight-mark answer on schools using facial recognition for lunch payments.
stations.fact: To answer an impact question, I should...

final.name: Final challenge: sort the impacts
final.intro: Eight concerns about new technologies. Tap the star and sort each into the kind of impact it is.

info.title: Why this topic exists
info.text: Every specification now includes impacts, because the people building systems are the ones who decide what gets built. The technical skill is only half the job.

info.title: Trolley problems
info.text: Driverless cars force a decision nobody wants to write down: who a car should protect in a crash. Engineers really do have to choose.

info.title: Marks for arguing
info.text: Impact questions are among the highest-mark questions on the paper, and the marks are for reasoning rather than recall.

info.title: Stakeholders in law
info.text: Big public projects legally require consultation with the people affected, which is stakeholder analysis by another name.

info.title: Piracy figures
info.text: Studies on lost income disagree wildly, partly because not every copy would have been a sale. Be careful quoting numbers you can't check.

info.title: Your turn
info.text: Every technology you use was signed off by someone. The questions in this topic are the ones they were asked.

exam.q: State two kinds of impact that should be considered before a new technology is introduced.
Explain what is meant by a stakeholder, using an example.
A council plans to put cameras with facial recognition in the town centre. Discuss the impacts of this decision.

title: Privacy lab
kicker: 1.6 Ethical, legal, cultural and environmental impacts  |  Lesson 2
subtitle: OCR J277 Paper 1  |  Computer systems
intro: What is collected about you, who gets it, and where the line between useful and intrusive sits.
objectives: understand at least one issue related to privacy and computer technology
be able to weigh the benefits and risks of collecting personal data
starter: List everything your phone knows about you that you never typed into it. How did it learn each one?
keyq: What privacy issues does computing create, and where should the limits be?

stations.name: What is collected
bullets: Personal data is anything that identifies you, on its own or combined with something else.
Typical collection: what you search, where you go, who you message, how long you look at something.
Data is valuable because it predicts what you will do next.
stations.challenge: List five pieces of data a social media app collects that you never typed in.

stations.name: Tracking
bullets: Cookies and identifiers follow a device from site to site, building a profile.
Apps can request location, contacts, microphone and camera, often for features that don't need them.
A profile built from many small facts can be more revealing than any single one.
stations.challenge: Why is a list of the places you visited more revealing than your address?

stations.name: Consent
bullets: Consent should be informed, freely given and easy to withdraw.
In practice it is often a long notice nobody reads, or a design that makes refusing hard.
Children's data has stronger protection in law, because consent is harder to give meaningfully.
stations.challenge: Rewrite a cookie banner so consent would actually be informed.

stations.name: Two sides of privacy
bullets: Collecting data does bring real benefits: better services, safety features, fraud detection, research.
It also brings risks: profiling, discrimination, breaches, and being watched.
Almost every privacy question is a trade-off, not a villain.
stations.challenge: Give one genuine benefit and one genuine risk of a phone tracking your location.

stations.name: When it goes wrong
bullets: A data breach exposes data that was collected for a legitimate reason.
The harm is real: fraud, blackmail, and details that cannot be made private again.
The best protection is not collecting what isn't needed, and deleting what is no longer used.
stations.challenge: Explain why deleting old data is a privacy measure, not just housekeeping.

stations.name: Arguing a privacy case
bullets: Name what is collected, who gets it, and what could go wrong.
Weigh the benefit against the risk for each stakeholder.
Conclude with a limit you can defend: what should be allowed, and what shouldn't.
stations.challenge: Plan an answer on smart speakers listening in a family home.
stations.fact: To argue a privacy question, I should...

final.name: Final challenge: the privacy line
final.intro: Eight practices. Tap the star and decide whether each is reasonable, needs clear consent, or goes too far.

info.title: The price of free
info.text: If a service is free, the running costs are usually paid for by advertising, and advertising is paid for by what is known about you.

info.title: Anonymous isn't
info.text: Studies have shown that a few 'anonymous' details, such as postcode, date of birth and sex, identify most people uniquely.

info.title: Metadata matters
info.text: Who you called and when can reveal more than the conversation itself: a call to a clinic followed by a call to a relative tells a story.

info.title: Dark patterns
info.text: Designs that make accepting easy and refusing hard have a name, and regulators have started fining companies for them.

info.title: Right to be forgotten
info.text: In the UK and EU you can ask for personal data to be deleted in many circumstances, though not where there's a legal reason to keep it.

info.title: Check your settings
info.text: Every phone has a screen listing which apps have location, microphone and camera access. Most people are surprised by it.

exam.q: State what is meant by personal data.
Describe one benefit and one risk of an app collecting location data.
A supermarket wants to use facial recognition to identify shoplifters. Discuss the privacy issues raised.

confidence: Arguing where the privacy line sits

title: Law court
kicker: 1.6 Ethical, legal, cultural and environmental impacts  |  Lesson 3
subtitle: OCR J277 Paper 1  |  Computer systems
intro: The three Acts you need: data protection, computer misuse, and copyright, and which one applies.
objectives: know the principles of the Data Protection Act 2018
know the principles of the Computer Misuse Act 1990
know the principles of the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988
starter: A pupil finds a teacher's password written on a desk and uses it to read a mark sheet. Which laws, if any, have been broken? Write your first thoughts.
keyterms: Data Protection Act 2018 Computer Misuse Act 1990

stations.name: Data Protection Act 2018
bullets: Governs how organisations collect, store and use personal data.
Data must be used fairly and lawfully, for a stated purpose, kept accurate, kept no longer than needed, and kept secure.
People have rights: to see their data, to correct it, and in many cases to have it deleted.
stations.challenge: State three things the Data Protection Act requires of an organisation.

stations.name: Computer Misuse Act 1990
bullets: Created to deal with hacking, which no earlier law covered.
Three main offences: unauthorised access; unauthorised access with intent to commit a further offence; unauthorised modification of data.
Access without permission is an offence even if nothing is changed or taken.
stations.challenge: Explain why guessing a friend's password and logging in is an offence even if you change nothing.
stations.fact: The Computer Misuse Act 1990 makes it an offence to...

stations.name: Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988
bullets: Protects the creator of original work: software, music, film, writing, images.
Copying, sharing or selling without permission infringes copyright.
It applies automatically the moment work is created: no registration needed.
stations.challenge: Explain why using an image from a web search in a book you sell is a problem.
stations.fact: The Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 protects...

stations.name: Which Act applies?
bullets: Personal data misused or leaked: Data Protection Act.
Access, hacking or changing data without permission: Computer Misuse Act.
Copying or sharing someone's creative work: Copyright, Designs and Patents Act.
stations.challenge: Sort six scenarios into the right Act, with a reason for each.
stations.fact: To decide which Act applies, ask...

stations.name: Other legislation
bullets: Freedom of Information allows anyone to request information held by public bodies, such as what a council spent.
It covers public information, not personal data about individuals.
Health and safety, equality and consumer law also apply to technology.
stations.challenge: Which law would you use to find out what a council paid for a new traffic system?

stations.name: Answering legal questions
bullets: Name the Act in full, including the year, then state the relevant principle.
Say which part of the situation breaches it.
If more than one Act applies, say so: many real cases involve two.
stations.challenge: Write a full answer to: a worker copies the customer database before leaving for a rival.

final.name: Final challenge: name the Act
final.intro: Nine cases have reached the court. Tap the star and decide which Act each one falls under.

info.title: Why 1990
info.text: The Computer Misuse Act was passed after two hackers who broke into a mailbox system were acquitted, because no existing law covered what they had done.

info.title: Fines that hurt
info.text: Serious data protection breaches can be fined up to 4% of a company's worldwide turnover, which is why boards now pay attention.

info.title: Copyright lasts
info.text: In the UK, copyright in a literary or musical work lasts for the creator's lifetime plus 70 years.

info.title: Not all copying is illegal
info.text: Limited copying for criticism, review, news reporting or education can be allowed under fair dealing, but the rules are narrower than most people assume.

info.title: Public bodies only
info.text: Freedom of Information covers councils, schools, the NHS and government departments, not private companies.

info.title: Licences everywhere
info.text: Every piece of software you use came with a licence setting out what you may do with it. Section 7 of this topic is about what those licences say.

exam.q: State two principles of the Data Protection Act 2018.
Describe the three offences under the Computer Misuse Act 1990.
A company finds that an employee has copied its customer database and taken it to a competitor. Explain which laws may have been broken.

title: Culture street
kicker: 1.6 Ethical, legal, cultural and environmental impacts  |  Lesson 4
subtitle: OCR J277 Paper 1  |  Computer systems
intro: How technology changed daily life, who gets left behind, and what globalisation did to work.
objectives: understand the impact of technology on daily life
starter: List five things your grandparents did differently at your age because the technology did not exist. Who gained and who lost from each change?
keyq: How does computing affect how people live and work?

stations.name: Technology and daily life
bullets: Shopping, banking, learning, healthcare and government moved online within a generation.
That is faster and cheaper for people who can get online.
Services that used to have a counter or a phone line increasingly have neither.
stations.challenge: Name three things you can now only do easily online, and say who that excludes.

stations.name: The digital divide
bullets: The digital divide is the gap between people who have good access to technology and those who don't.
Causes: cost of devices and data, poor broadband, age, disability, and skills.
Effects: worse access to education, jobs, cheaper prices and public services.
stations.challenge: Name three causes of the digital divide and one effect of each.

stations.name: Closing the gap
bullets: Public wifi, libraries and school device loans widen access.
Subsidised connections and low-cost devices lower the cost barrier.
Training matters as much as hardware: a device nobody can use helps nobody.
stations.challenge: Suggest three things a town could do to narrow its digital divide.
stations.fact: The digital divide can be narrowed by...

stations.name: Globalisation
bullets: Networks let a company work across many countries at once, around the clock.
Work can be done wherever it is cheapest, which creates jobs in some places and removes them in others.
Culture travels too: the same films, games and platforms reach almost everywhere.
stations.challenge: Give one benefit and one drawback of globalisation for a UK worker.

stations.name: Work and automation
bullets: Remote working spread when networks made it practical, changing commuting, offices and town centres.
Automation removes repetitive jobs and creates different ones, usually needing different skills.
The people who lose a job are rarely the ones who get the new one.
stations.challenge: Name one job changed by automation in your lifetime, and say how.

stations.name: Answering cultural questions
bullets: Name the group affected before saying how.
Use the words the specification uses: digital divide, globalisation, automation, access.
Discuss means both sides, then a conclusion you can defend.
stations.challenge: Plan an eight-mark answer on a bank closing its last local branch.
stations.fact: To answer a cultural question, I should...

final.name: Final challenge: who is left behind?
final.intro: Eight statements about cultural change. Tap the star and sort each one.

info.title: Not just rural
info.text: The divide is often sharpest within cities, where cost rather than coverage is the barrier.

info.title: Homework gap
info.text: During school closures, the difference between pupils with a laptop and those without became one of the clearest examples of the divide.

info.title: Follow the sun
info.text: Global firms pass work between offices in different time zones so a project is worked on continuously.

info.title: Not new
info.text: Every wave of technology has moved work: looms, production lines, spreadsheets. What changes is how fast and which jobs.

info.title: Language online
info.text: A small number of languages dominate the web, which pushes speakers of smaller languages towards them.

info.title: The 15-minute answer
info.text: Examiners say cultural questions are often answered with opinion and no reasons. Reasons are where the marks are.

exam.q: State what is meant by the digital divide.
Describe two ways globalisation has been made possible by computer networks.
A council moves all its services online. Discuss the cultural impacts of this decision.

title: Planet works
kicker: 1.6 Ethical, legal, cultural and environmental impacts  |  Lesson 5
subtitle: OCR J277 Paper 1  |  Computer systems
intro: The environmental cost of a device across its whole life: making it, running it and throwing it away.
objectives: understand the environmental impact of manufacturing computers
understand the environmental impact of using computers
understand the environmental impact of disposing of computers
starter: Think of the last device your household replaced. Where did the old one go, and what was it made from?
keyq: What is the environmental impact of computing, across a device's whole life?

stations.name: Three stages
bullets: Every device has an environmental cost at three stages: manufacture, use and disposal.
For a phone, manufacture is usually the largest share by far.
Judging a device on its running cost alone misses most of its impact.
stations.challenge: Name the three stages and give one impact at each.
stations.fact: The three stages of impact are...

stations.name: Making it
bullets: Devices need metals that are mined, including rare earth elements, gold, copper and lithium.
Mining and refining use energy and water, and can pollute land and rivers.
Some materials come from areas with poor working conditions or conflict.
stations.challenge: Explain why the materials in a phone raise ethical as well as environmental issues.

stations.name: Using it
bullets: Devices use electricity, and so do the networks and data centres behind them.
Streaming, cloud storage and AI all move the energy cost from your device to a building somewhere else.
Where the electricity comes from decides how much carbon that energy represents.
stations.challenge: Explain why watching a video 'uses no energy on your phone' is misleading.
stations.fact: Using a device costs the environment because...

stations.name: Throwing it away
bullets: Electronic waste is the fastest growing waste stream in the world.
Devices contain toxic materials: lead, mercury, cadmium. In landfill these leak into soil and water.
Much e-waste is shipped abroad and stripped by hand, often in unsafe conditions.
stations.challenge: Explain why e-waste is an ethical issue as well as an environmental one.

stations.name: Doing better
bullets: Repair, reuse and upgrade extend a device's life, which is the biggest single saving.
Proper recycling recovers metals so they need not be mined again.
Designing for repair, and laws requiring spare parts, change what is possible.
stations.challenge: Suggest three things a school could do to cut the environmental impact of its computers.
stations.fact: The impact can be reduced by...

stations.name: Answering environmental questions
bullets: Say which stage you mean: manufacture, use or disposal.
Give the mechanism, not just the label: what is used, emitted or leaked, and why that matters.
Where there is a trade-off, name it: recycling costs money, longer life means older technology.
stations.challenge: Plan a six-mark answer on a school replacing all its computers every three years.
stations.fact: To answer an environmental question, I should...

final.name: Final challenge: the whole life
final.intro: Nine impacts from a device's life. Tap the star and sort each into the stage it belongs to.

info.title: Most of it is made, not used
info.text: For a typical smartphone, manufacturing accounts for roughly three quarters of its lifetime carbon.

info.title: Gold in the bin
info.text: A tonne of discarded phones contains far more gold than a tonne of ore from a mine, which is why recycling them properly is worth doing.

info.title: Right to repair
info.text: Rules now require manufacturers of some products to supply spare parts for several years, driven exactly by the argument in this lesson.

info.title: Data centre thirst
info.text: Large data centres use water as well as electricity for cooling, which has become contentious in dry regions.

info.title: E-waste scale
info.text: Tens of millions of tonnes of electronic waste are produced each year, and only a fraction is formally recycled.

info.title: The best upgrade
info.text: Adding memory or an SSD to an older machine costs a fraction of the carbon of a new one, and is often the bigger speed gain.

exam.q: State two environmental impacts of manufacturing a computer.
Explain why electronic waste is a problem when sent to landfill.
A school replaces all of its computers every three years. Discuss the environmental impact of this policy.

confidence: Impacts of use, including data centres

title: Stakeholder room
kicker: 1.6 Ethical, legal, cultural and environmental impacts  |  Lesson 6
subtitle: OCR J277 Paper 1  |  Computer systems
intro: Reading a scenario the way an examiner does: who the stakeholders are, and the local, national and global effects.
objectives: be able to identify key stakeholders
be able to consider a scenario from the perspective of stakeholders
understand impacts at local, national and global levels
starter: A supermarket announces that all its tills will be self-service within a year. List everyone affected, and one effect each.
keyq: How does digital technology affect society locally, nationally and globally?

stations.name: Finding the stakeholders
bullets: Ask who uses it, who runs it, who pays for it, and who is affected without choosing to be.
The last group is the one students forget, and often where the marks are.
List them before writing anything else.
stations.challenge: For a town installing smart traffic lights, list six stakeholders.

stations.name: Local, national, global
bullets: Local: this street, this school, this town.
National: jobs, laws, infrastructure and services across the country.
Global: supply chains, emissions, and where the work and waste actually go.
stations.challenge: Give a local, national and global impact of online shopping.

stations.name: Working a scenario
bullets: Read the scenario twice: once for what changes, once for who it touches.
For each stakeholder, ask what they gain, what they lose, and what they now have to do differently.
Then decide which impacts are big enough to write about.
stations.challenge: Work through the smart meter scenario in the experience and record your reasons.

stations.name: Trade-offs
bullets: Almost every scenario has a genuine benefit and a genuine cost.
Answers that only attack, or only praise, lose marks.
State the trade-off plainly: what is gained, at whose expense.
stations.challenge: Write the trade-off in one sentence for driverless delivery vehicles.

stations.name: Reaching a conclusion
bullets: A conclusion is a position, not a summary.
Say what should happen, and which argument decided it for you.
A condition is often the strongest conclusion: yes, provided that…
stations.challenge: Write a conclusion on smart meters that includes a condition.

stations.name: Practice scenario
bullets: A hospital replaces paper notes with tablets carried by every nurse.
Stakeholders: patients, nurses, doctors, IT staff, administrators, the trust's finances.
Impacts run from bedside to national policy.
stations.challenge: Work the hospital scenario fully on your worksheet.
stations.fact: In this scenario, the impacts are...

final.name: Final challenge: the smart town
final.intro: A town installs sensors that track traffic, air quality and parking. Tap the star and work the scenario.

info.title: Stakeholder is a real job
info.text: Large projects employ people whose entire role is consulting the groups a change will affect.

info.title: Unintended effects
info.text: Ride-hailing apps cut waiting times and also changed congestion, taxi licensing and public transport use in ways nobody planned.

info.title: Smart meter rollout
info.text: Britain's smart meter programme is one of the largest technology rollouts ever attempted here, and it has had every impact in this lesson.

info.title: Who pays?
info.text: A common exam trick: the group that benefits and the group that pays are different. Say so.

info.title: Conditions score
info.text: Conclusions with a condition attached usually read as more thoughtful than a flat yes or no.

info.title: Try it on anything
info.text: The method works on any scenario: streaming, self-checkouts, AI marking, electric cars, school fingerprint systems.

exam.q: State what is meant by a stakeholder.
A town installs sensors to monitor traffic and air quality. Identify three stakeholders and describe one impact on each.
Discuss the impacts of replacing supermarket checkout staff with self-service machines.

title: Licence lab
kicker: 1.6 Ethical, legal, cultural and environmental impacts  |  Lesson 7
subtitle: OCR J277 Paper 1  |  Computer systems
intro: Open source and proprietary software: what each licence allows, and which suits a given situation.
objectives: understand the difference between open source and proprietary software
understand the implications of using open source and proprietary software
starter: List five programs you use. For each, say whether you think its source code is published, and whether anyone paid for it.
keyq: What are the implications of choosing open source or proprietary software?

stations.name: What a licence decides
bullets: A software licence sets out what you may do with the program: use it, copy it, change it, share it.
Buying software usually buys a licence to use it, not ownership of it.
Breaking the licence terms is a copyright matter, from lesson 3.
stations.challenge: Explain the difference between owning software and owning a licence to use it.

stations.name: Proprietary software
bullets: The source code is kept secret and cannot be modified by users.
Usually paid for, with a licence limiting how many machines or users.
Comes with professional support, tested releases and, often, training and warranties.
stations.challenge: Name three proprietary programs used in your school and say who supports them.

stations.name: Open source software
bullets: The source code is published, and may be used, changed and shared under the licence terms.
Usually free of charge, though not always.
Support comes from the community, or from a company paid to provide it.
stations.challenge: Give two advantages and two drawbacks of open source software for a school.

stations.name: Support and cost
bullets: Proprietary: licence fees, but support is part of the deal.
Open source: no licence fee, but you may need staff who can maintain it, or a paid support contract.
Free to download is not the same as free to run.
stations.challenge: Explain why free software can still cost an organisation money.

stations.name: Choosing between them
bullets: Think about budget, the skills available, how critical the system is, and whether it must be adapted.
Critical systems with no in-house expertise point to proprietary; tight budgets with technical staff point to open source.
Many organisations run both, choosing per job.
stations.challenge: Recommend a licence type for a primary school, a hospital and a games studio, with reasons.
stations.fact: To choose a licence type, ask...

stations.name: Common misconceptions
bullets: Open source does not mean unlicensed: the licence still sets conditions.
Open source is not automatically less secure, nor automatically more secure.
Proprietary does not always mean paid, and free does not always mean open source.
stations.challenge: Correct this statement: 'Open source software is free software with no rules.'

final.name: Final challenge: pick the licence
final.intro: Eight statements and situations. Tap the star and sort each one.

info.title: Open source runs the internet
info.text: Most web servers, and the software behind most websites, are open source. So is the code inside most phones.

info.title: Licences differ
info.text: Some open source licences let you do almost anything; others require you to publish your changes. Reading the licence matters.

info.title: Paid open source
info.text: Companies sell supported versions of open source software: the code is free, the support contract is not.

info.title: Security both ways
info.text: Open code lets more people find flaws, including attackers. Closed code hides flaws from everyone, including defenders.

info.title: Schools and cost
info.text: Licensing is one of the largest lines in a school's IT budget, which is why the question comes up in real life as well as exams.

info.title: Lock-in
info.text: The cost of leaving a supplier, because your data and workflows are tied to their software, is called lock-in, and it is a real argument for open formats.

exam.q: State one difference between open source and proprietary software.
Describe two advantages of open source software for a school.
A hospital is choosing between open source and proprietary software for its patient record system. Recommend one and justify your choice.
